thread.title: Top Holdings Of Dividend ETFs (Part 1: The Top 50)

author: FerdiS
title: Top Holdings Of Dividend ETFs (Part 1: The Top 50)
text:
From time to time, I compile a virtual portfolio of the top holdings of Dividend ETFs. I find the exercise insightful and certainly worth the effort. Comparing my portfolio to the virtual portfolio is informative, as it helps me to identify candidate stocks for analysis and possible investment.
Below, I'll provide a brief summary of the methodology. For a detailed description, please refer to previous editions in this series:
Top Holdings of Dividend ETFs (June 2018 Edition) Top Holdings of Dividend ETFs (November 2017 Edition) Top Holdings of Dividend ETFs (June 2017 Edition) Top Holdings of Dividend ETFs — published in December 2016 I have published similar articles using Real Estate ETFs and the public portfolios of Dividend Growth Bloggers as data sources.
Dividend ETF Analysis Dividend ETFs invest in stocks that pay dividends and regularly increase them. The issuers of ETFs provide data about each ETF's holdings, typically the ticker symbol, company name, the percentage of assets under management allocated to each holding, and the market value of the holding.
I collect these data from established Dividend ETFs and compile a spreadsheet with tickers of the top 25 holdings in each ETF, along with the market value of each holding. To rank the top holdings, I use the relative market value of each holding to score the corresponding ticker. This is a proportional scoring system that favors larger investments over smaller ones within the same ETF.
Then I assign weights to each ETF based on the total assets under management. Rather than doing so proportionally, I use a log -based formula:
w = floor ( log 10 (assets in millions))
ETFs with assets under $100 million get a weight of 1. ETFs with assets under $1,000 million (but ≥ $100 million) get a weight of 2. ETFs with assets under $10,000 million (but ≥ $1,000 million) get a weight of 3. ETFs with assets under $100,000 million (but ≥ $10,000 million) get a weight of 4. With proportional scores assigned to each ticker per ETF and weights assigned to each ETF, I simply calculate a weighted sum to get an aggregate score for each ticker. Sorting the aggregate scores in descending order determines the rank of each stock (ticker).
Note that I exclude stocks that don't pay dividends. For example, I excluded stocks like Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), and Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.B ) (NYSE: BRK.A ) from consideration, even though these stocks made the top 50 list based on aggregate score.
The Dividend ETF Database I used ETFdb's screener to identify Dividend ETFs for this analysis, limiting the search to Dividend ETFs in North America that have positive 3-year returns. The following table lists 47 ETFs, sorted by assets under management (in millions of dollars). The data source is ETFdb and the data presented in the table were extracted on 12 November 2018:
The Top 50 Holdings The following chart presents the top 50 holdings ranked by aggregate score. The tickers are color-coded by GICS sector.
Note that the GICS sectors recently changed and that ETFs are being impacted by these changes. Most notably, the Telecommunications Services sector is being expanded to become the Communications Services sector and includes some stocks previously classified as Information Technology and Consumer Discretionary stocks.
Exxon Mobil ( XOM ) is the clear winner, followed by Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ). XOM appeared in the top 25 holdings of 23 of the 47 Dividend ETFs analyzed.
Note that not a single Materials sector stock is in the top 50 holdings. Here is a pie chart showing the distribution of stocks by GICS sector:
The following table presents key metrics of the top 50 holdings. Rank is the stock's position when ranked by aggregate score. Freq indicates the number of dividend ETFs containing Ticker in their top 25 holdings. Years are the number of consecutive years of dividend increases. Yield is the dividend yield, and 5-DGR is the compound annual dividend growth rate over a 5-year period.
Stocks I own in my DivGro portfolio are highlighted.

As a virtual portfolio, the top 50 holdings have a dividend yield of 3.5% and would have returned about 14% over the past year. Comparing the 5-year performance of the top 50 holdings to that of the S&P 500, we note that the top 50 holdings outperformed the S&P 500 by about 29%.
Changes Since Last Time There are a few changes in the top 10 when compared with June's edition. In fact, only one stock dropped out of the top 10 (WFC) and was replaced by another (KO). WFC dropped 6 places to #15, whereas KO climbed 9 places from #19. The remaining changes in the top 10 are positional shuffling:

How Does Your Portfolio Compare? Dividend growth investors may find it interesting to compare their own portfolios to the top 50 holdings of Dividend ETFs. Are there any surprises? How many of the top 50 stocks do you own?
Comparing my DivGro portfolio of 80 different positions to the top 50 holdings, I count 9 DivGro stocks in the top 10 and 15 stocks in the top 20. A total of 30 DivGro stocks are in the top 50 holdings.
If "only" 30 of my stocks are in the top 50, then 50 stocks are not. Here is the list of stocks in DivGro that are ranked but fall outside of the top 50:
Starbucks ( SBUX ) — #51 WEC Energy ( WEC ) — #53 NextEra Energy ( NEE ) — #54 Qualcomm ( QCOM ) — #55 Simon Property Group ( SPG ) — #61 Eversource Energy ( ES ) — #64 Federal Realty ( FRT ) — #69 Xcel Energy ( XEL ) — #75 Amgen ( AMGN ) — #77 Walgreens Boots Alliance ( WBA ) — #83 Tanger Factor Outlet Centers ( SKT ) — #87 TJX ( TJX ) — #101 Illinois Tool Works ( ITW ) — #106 Medtronic ( MDT ) — #110 National Retail Properties ( NNN ) — #112 Lowe's ( LOW ) — #115 Gilead Sciences ( GILD ) — #120 Hormel Foods ( HRL ) — #127 Nike ( NKE ) — #129 Nvidia ( NVDA ) — #149 United Parcel Service ( UPS ) — #164 Travelers ( TRV ) — #176 Stanley Black & Decker ( SWK ) — #198 A few stocks barely missed making the top 50 list, notably SBUX (#51), WEC (#53), NEE (#54), and QCOM (#55). In all, 53 of my DivGro stocks are ranked.
On the other hand, the following stocks in my portfolio are nowhere to be found in any of the top 25s:
Chubb ( CB ) Quest Diagnostics ( DGX ) Cummins ( CMI ) Digital Realty Trust ( DLR ) EPR Properties ( EPR ) Extra Space Storage ( EXR ) KB Home ( KBH ) Kite Realty ( KRG ) Main Street Capital ( MAIN ) Netflix ( NFLX ) Omega Healthcare Investors ( OHI ) T. Rowe Price ( TROW ) Xilinx ( XLNX ) DLR, EPR, EXR, KRG, and OHI are REITs (real estate investment trusts), which have their own category at ETFdb. And MAIN is organized as a business development company, which also has its own category at ETFdb.
Additionally, I own a few non-dividend paying stocks, one exchange-traded fund ( VYM ), and one closed-end fund.
Concluding Remarks Analyzing the holdings of Dividend ETFs is an insightful exercise. Publicly-available data on the top holdings and assets under management allows one to rank these holdings and to create a list of dividend growth stocks worthy of consideration.
Please note that I'm not recommending any of the top 50 holdings. Many of these stocks are trading above fair value and may not be suitable for investment at this time. Before investing in any of these stocks, please do a thorough analysis to determine if the stocks are worthy of your investment dollars.
Apart from VYM, I don't own any other ETFs. Investing in ETFs provides several benefits, including instant diversification and passive investment. However, you have no control over the makeup of the ETF or its turnover rate. The investment manager determines the ETF's makeup and trading frequency and charges a recurring annual fee called the ETF's expense ratio.
In Part 2 of this article, I'll showcase the top 10 stocks in each GICS sector. Looking at the ranked stocks outside of the top 50 provides additional insight. Because there are no Materials sector stocks in the top 50, it would be useful to see the top-ranked Material sector stocks regardless of overall ranking. Investors looking to build a diversified portfolio might find such information useful.
